The second is that he and all the other senior representatives of the Republika Srpska were continually seeking recognition that they existed as an independent entity, and therefore they were very particular that the formalities and the appellations and so on were as if they were recognising the existence of Republika Srpska as an independent entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that was a theme that was not only mentioned by Mladic, but also was mentioned by Karadzic in meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And one of the things that happened - and once again for the moment I'm just speaking generally with regard to meetings - one of the things that occurred at least on one occasion if not more is that when a specific request for something to occur was asked of Mladic, he would defer to his president?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at times when a specific request was asked of Karadzic, he would defer to his assembly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in those situations, they were indicating to you that there was a political process that existed that had to be respected internally; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were continually trying to emphasise that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And also that there was a relationship between the military component that was headed by General Mladic and the political executive component that was headed by Dr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they tried to maintain that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously with regard to meetings that you had with such individual as Mladic and Karadzic, these were of critical importance to note?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You testified, as I understand it that the first meeting that you had with Mladic, Karadzic, and others was on the 27th of October; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that was a meeting -- that was a meeting that, as I understand it, not from your testimony yesterday but from your -- from some other documents that I've read, was a meeting that dealt with the issue, among others, that dealt with the issue of cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it dealt with a whole range of issues, as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the day before on the 26th, you had met with Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe on the 26th, I said 25th, 26th was when we arrived in Sarajevo. And it was the next day that we first met in -- first met with Mladic. Having said that, General Morillon, I believe, had met with Mladic previously in his previous role as deputy command of UNPROFOR in Krajina, but I don't know any details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. With regard to the first time that you met General Mladic, was that in the presence of Karadzic? That was all together; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was all together. I would need to check my notes. The main thing that I recollect of that meeting was that it was with Mladic in Lukavica and Mladic was being very insistent. He started the meeting off by demanding that all communication to the to him be addressed to Republika Srpska Krajina. General Morillon stated that he had sent a letter to Madam Plavsic in order to try and expedite permission to deploy the Canadian battalion and permission to deploy the French battalion in Petrovac. Mladic told General Morillon that he made a big mistake in approaching, in writing to Madam Plavsic, Madam --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you. And I thank you for your answer because I think it's all quite interesting, but my question was, Was that in the presence of Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check my notes in order to confirm that precisely on that specific day because as I said, that was 17 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, I am sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, we've been throwing around dates of 26th, 27th October. Just so that we don't have to look elsewhere in the transcript for the year, can we just give it a year, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be 1992 that we are referring to; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I note that you indicated that all communications to him be addressed to the Republika Srpska Krajina, and --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I think you may have misspoke and you meant the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Morillon asked him, What about the Krajina? And Mladic said, That's a separate republic; that's the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You'll recall in your testimony yesterday you indicated that in the first meeting that Karadzic was present. And the reason I'm trying to get an understanding of this is that was the meeting in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting with Mladic on the 27th was in Lukavica. The meeting at which Karadzic was present and Professor Koljevic, the one where I referred to the census map, that took place in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So that would have been the next day, the 28th? Let me see if I can be of some help to you here, and I'm going to read you something and see whether or not this is of any help to you. And I'm reading from the statement that you gave. This is only for purposes of refreshing your recollection. This is the statement that you gave on the 6th and 7th of September, 2000; the 27th of July, 2001, and the 5th and 6th of March, 2002. And you say: "General Morillon's first appeal to the RS leaders to secure deployment of CanBat was in a form of a letter to Mrs. Plavsic which he wrote on 27 October 1992." Which I think you had just discussed. "At that time we thought she was more influential, and we later found out she was. The same day, I what present at a meeting between General Mladic and General Morillon. This meeting took place in Lukavica. I have some photographs that were taken after its conclusion. This was my first meeting with Mladic. Karadzic was in Geneva." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Karadzic was in Geneva for at least ten days or so, and in fact we believed that Mladic took advantage of the fact that Karadzic was in Geneva in order to launch his last attack on Sarajevo in order to try and capture or cut Sarajevo in half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, as I understand the first meeting, that meeting dealt with CanBat 2 deployment to the Banja Luka area; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mladic informed you that he did not have the authority to agree to this, but he would discuss this with the government?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said it was a matter for the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. During that meeting, Mladic and Morillon also discussed the issue of freedom of movement for UNPROFOR and UNHCR convoys generally?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And also was discussed the issue of demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that the issue of demilitarisation was discussed, could you please just briefly for the moment, because we will be discussing it later again, touch upon what was discussed with regard to the issue of demilitarisation as it related to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two dimensions to demilitarisation. One was Sarajevo itself, and the lifting of the siege. Mladic refused to use the language or accept the language siege or surrounded. What Mladic insisted was that he was merely holding his own terrain and protecting his own people inside his own terrain. He said that if the Muslims were either willing to hand all their weapons to the -- in Sarajevo - this is to the United Nations - or were willing to allow Serb -- Bosnian Serb police into Sarajevo, that then he was willing to allow freedom of movement in and out for all. On the second issue was heavy weapons, and when General Morillon asked Mladic about his heavy weapons and requested Mladic to remove his heavy weapons away from around Sarajevo, Mladic's response was that he was willing to do so providing that the Muslims handed all their weapons over to the United Nations and disarmed. If you want specific detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, that's fine for the moment because there's -- as I think we both understand, there's a further discussion, specifically about demilitarisation with Oric when you are in Srebrenica, and there's a further discussion with the war committee about demilitarisation as a manner of solution when you are in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is a different aspect once again to that matter. What you've mentioned here is one of the tensions, I think, that did occur, and the analysis, as I understand it, from a review of your documentation is that Mladic equated his heavy weapon use with the strength of the BiH Army's infantry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in a very real sense, what we had occurring at the time was that the Bosnian Serb Army had greater heavy weaponry; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the BiH Army had more infantry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had many more people. They were much more populace, but only armed with infantry weapons obviously, and not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, did you have at that time - I'm talking about the very first meeting - was there any discussion at that time about the concept of Territorial Defence that existed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the thing which I recall Mladic saying was that he was holding his own territory. He demanded that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He claimed the territory in order to defend his people. However, he did not at that time, I recall, talk about Territorial Defence or militia or anything like that, that only came up in much later conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before -- okay. Before you came to Sarajevo, were you aware of the -- of the manner in which the former Yugoslavia had determined how to defend itself in case of incursions after World War II? And just briefly here because I don't want to get into a long history discussion, briefly here, Tito had created not only an army, but it created the concept of Territorial Defence where every able-bodied man between a certain ages was available for fighting for the Defence of not only their country, but also their specific region; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. And it's also the context in which Bosnia-Herzegovina was the arms depot of the former Yugoslavia because of its mountainous terrain, in the centre, in the heart of the former Yugoslavia. And it was western intelligence assessments that the vast bulk of the ammunition and equipment which was stockpiled in -- on the ground bunkers and depots was within Bosnia-Herzegovina and that that was one of the reasons why western intelligence assessment was that the Bosnian Serb Army had, and I think one of the quotes was, Had enough ammunition to continue the combat operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the intensity that they were going for a further ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue that you've just raised again which is western intelligence assessments, there once again we are talking about information that has been compiled and analysed upon which conclusions have been drawn, this conclusion being a conclusion with regard to the ability to wage war?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, are those reports that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were briefings we were given before we deployed into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So similar --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would have been September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So similar to the other situation, I take it there are no notes, it was oral, and you cannot remember who gave you this information; or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would have been briefings in Moenchengladbach before we departed and they were intelligence staff officers who participated. And as you can imagine, we were preparing for deployment; there were many things going on. And part of briefings were intelligence briefings and western intelligence was scrambling to pull together as much information as it could obviously prior to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, the answer to my question would be no notes and no identification of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the meeting with Mladic concerning cessation of hostilities and other things, but I'm going to focus on the cessation of hostilities because something -- as I understand it, the first meeting occurred, which is that although Mladic had called for the meeting, ultimately what occurred was that Bobetko signed, Mladic did not sign the cessation of hostilities agreement in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting with -- to be clear, this first meeting that I attended with Mladic on the 27th of October, nothing was signed. The meeting that Mladic eventually had with Bobetko was towards the end of November, and at that meeting Bobetko, if I remember, actually at the meeting, actually in a flourish signed the declaration. But Mladic refused to sign and left the meeting not having signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when Mladic did sign?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, but again would I need to check. I believe he signed it one or two days later or at a next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And what is -- for the Chamber's purposes, what is the effect of a signed cessation of hostilities agreement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Obviously there are two parts to this. Let me back up because I think your chuckle deals with a certain aspect. If followed, what would have been the effect of cessation hostilities agreement at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that once a leader or senior officer has signed a cessation of hostilities, that he would then issue orders within his chain of command in order to order his forces not to carry out conduct -- combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just as a general matter, can you tell the Chamber in your estimation how many cessation of hostilities/cease-fire agreements do you think you brokered during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many. How many? 10, 20, 30, I don't know. There were so many of them, and none them were ever adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "none of them were ever adhered to," would it be fair to say that both parties - and by that I mean the Bosnian Serbs and the Presidency as you called it - broke those cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All -- in my view all three parties, the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Croats, and the Bosnian Serbs broke cease-fire agreements when it suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in regard to the breaking of the cease-fire agreements, I think that you came to a position concerning cease-fire agreements in general. And I'm referring you to some prior testimony in which you stated: "We have been trying to negotiate cease-fire since we had arrived in Bosnia. There was a recurring theme to cease-fires, which was that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted a cease-fire or cease fires to cover all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words they wanted to consolidate their gain and consolidate what they had taken, whereas the Bosniak leadership declared that they wanted cease-fires." And I think that you should have said "they didn't" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we could please have the source of the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise. That's page 5795, lines 1 through 9 in IT-03-68-T. "The reality of the way they behaved was that whenever they were under pressure militarily from the Serbs, they wanted local cease-fires, but then contrived to try to break those cease-fires and provoke the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. What would happen is that the Bosnian Serb intent, as I described from the beginning, as I described General Mladic in his first meeting and in the meeting with Karadzic, they continually tried to emphasise, We want to be our own entity; we want the status quo to be recognised; we want recognition; we are -- we want a cease-fire across the whole front line. The Presidency publicly declared that they wanted a cease-fire as well. The practical reality was that they did not recognise the status quo and wanted to take back territory which had been seized by the Bosnian Serbs and therefore were carrying out local attacks. When those local attacks were eventually repulsed by the Bosnian Serbs because typically it took them a day or 2 to repulse them because the Bosnian Serbs were numerically weak all the way around this very long and tangled front line, the Muslims would usually make initial progress until such time as the Bosnian Serbs had first mustered heavy weapons against them. And secondly, if it was a serious incursion, had managed to move their reserves, their regular forces around in order to push the -- the incursion back in order to re-establish the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So it would be -- and I take it that this is something that you experienced from the time that you first arrived in October of 1992 until you left in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was another dimension to it, which was that our UN deployment in Bosnia was under Chapter 6. And under the remit to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid to those in need, our mandate was not to engage in the fighting. And it was a constant attempt by the Presidency to try and inveigle the United Nations forces in fighting on their side against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you've raised that particular matter which is the constant attempt by the Presidency which would be the Bosniak Muslims --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- to try and inveigle the United Nations forces in fighting on the other side against the Serbs. I would like to discuss with you for a moment an incident concerning mortar fire emanating from the Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo; do you know what I speak?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are referring to an incident when some UN forces, some UN personnel were delivering diesel fuel to the hospital saw a mobile detachment of light mortars who had deployed -- this is Bosniak -- Bosnian Muslim military inside Sarajevo who had deployed to the hospital and had fired from the grounds of the hospital at some forces surrounding Sarajevo, and then rapidly withdrew from the hospital. This was in the knowledge that the Bosnian Serbs surrounding Sarajevo had mortar-locating radar, that is radar of which is capable of seeing artillery shells mortar shells in the air, and from that calculating the location from where they had been fired because the Bosnian Serbs then immediately fired counter-battery fire as quickly as they could back at the location from which the outcoming fire had come. However, the location where this fire had come from was obviously Kosevo Hospital, so therefore when the incoming Serb counter-bombardment, as it were, came in, of course, it landed on Kosevo Hospital. And if I remember correctly, a press conference had been arranged by the Presidency at the hospital half an hour later, and effectively the incoming Serb fire landed on the hospital around the time of the start of the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say a press conference was called, who called that press conference?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of who called them --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant which -- I was asking a much more general question for the moment. Was that the Presidency that called it or the Bosniak --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somebody on the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you had information, if I'm not mistaken, that the head of the hospital was someone who not only supported the general cause of the Presidency, but was, I think, a radical hardliner?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm referring -- quoting, counsel, to IT-98-29-T page 10.022. These are questions that are being asked by Judge Nieto-Navia. In relation to what you've told us about firing coming from the surroundings of the Kosevo Hospital, you told us you received information from two sources. Do you recall receiving information from two sources? Firstly a British sergeant and then from journalists?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we may be mixing events up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, well, let's -- if we have more than one incident where there's been firing from the Kosevo Hospital, let's deal with them sequentially.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had reports, but unconfirmed, not much more than rumour, that mortars were being fired now and then from Kosevo Hospital. It was only when this -- this British sergeant physically saw it while he was delivering, that we had what we considered to be confirmed proof. And the instance about journalist was a totally second -- that's a totally different event which I believe is the one you may be referring to which is when some mortar rounds were fired at General Morillon's headquarters in Sarajevo, a location confusingly called the "Residency" as opposed to the "Presidency" which is where the government of the Bosnian Muslims was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that incident, when General Morillon's -- is that his home or his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His headquarters. Well, it was where we lived as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the incident concerning the residency involving the Bosniak side firing, could you tell us what the date was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there were two incidents. One was on the 24th of December, 1992, and the second was at dawn on Christmas day, the 25th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the Kosevo Hospital matter, Judge Nieto-Navia went on to ask you questions concerning whether or not you knew of any firings or mortars emanating from any other hospitals in Sarajevo, and I believe that you said that you did not, and then you went on to explain that the Kosevo Hospital is somewhat unique. Do you recall why the Kosevo Hospital was unique in regard to the issue of the ability to fire from such an area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about unique, but it looked to me like most other hospitals I know which are some large buildings and in between the buildings you have car parks and open space, and it was in this open space between the buildings that the mortars had been fired from as reported by the British sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And there was a third thing that I mentioned, which was the issue of the hardliner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now referring the Court and counsel to page 10.024.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You answer as follows to -- this is Judge El Madhi question with regard to other hospitals, I misspoke myself. You say starting at line 4: "I must answer in several steps. The first step is to say that I have no knowledge from such firing from the proximity of other hospitals in Sarajevo." Which we've just discussed. "Secondly, the other hospitals in Sarajevo were very different types of buildings." Which is why I alluded to the fact that the Kosevo was unique. "Kosevo Hospital was the only hospital which was spread out over quite a large area. The other hospitals were solid, single buildings with a building next to it maybe, so they did not lend themselves to the kind of tactic." And I think that's a kind of tactic that you've described that is available where you had a mobile mortar unit. And then you say: "The third thing is that the head of Kosevo Hospital was known to us as a radical hardliner and was someone who we believed would have certainly supported this kind of tactic in the greater interest as he saw it of supporting the Bosniak cause whereas the directors of the other hospitals were, in our view, much more medically focused and refused to have anything to do with the kind of action that the director of the Kosevo Hospital, in our view, participated in." And that was what I was referring to when I mentioned there was a hardliner. Do you, by any chance, recall the name of the director of the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you've refreshed my memory on that, I do recollect there was something about the head of the Kosevo Hospital. I can't remember here now what his name is. It's possible that it might be mentioned in my notes, but I would -- I would have no idea where it is without spending a long time trolling through my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we were on the issue of hospitals, one of the other matters brought to your attention was the smuggling of explosives in oxygen bottles to the hospitals; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, oxygen bottles would be, if I'm not mistaken, certainly a form of humanitarian aid, and certainly something that would be critical and necessary for a functioning of a hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate in your view for explosives to be smuggled into a hospital through the use of oxygen bottles which ostensibly are being delivered for purposes of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a breach of the agreements between the warring factions and with the United Nations to smuggle explosives or weapons of any form hidden inside humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of explosives being found in a delivery of what is ostensibly humanitarian aid, would that be, in your view, a basis upon which it would be reasonable to search a convoy that is, and I'm using the word "claiming" not in a pejorative sense, but claiming to be delivering solely humanitarian aid, with that as an experience?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now speaking personally. I would have an understanding for that desire, but I would also maintain that regardless, such searches should not in any way, shape, or form be used in order to prevent humanitarian aid from getting through or getting through at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's my point, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, but that's not my question, sir. My question is that given that it would be inappropriate to be using humanitarian aid for a military purpose, would it not be reasonable to search the convoy? I'm not getting any further than that at the moment, and we'll have further discussions about convoys and searches and stopping in -- after the break, but would that be an unreasonable thing to do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing that it did not be used as an excuse to stop the aid getting through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So, if you were aware that a humanitarian aid convoy contained weapons, it is your position - so we're clear - it's your position that the convoy should go through --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was our position that no weapons should be allowed through, and we -- whenever we became aware or had suspicions that weapons might be hidden in humanitarian aid, we searched them ourselves as well. And on a number of occasions, we found weapons and made the strongest protest to whichever side was responsible for placing those weapons in the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as a matter of reality, the strong protests that were made, be they to one side or the other as we've discussed cease-fires, often fell on deaf ears; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like most requests for humanity in that part of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would indeed be. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought I did say yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to go back now for a moment and deal with some chronology dates if I could. And as I understood it, around the 31st of October, 1992, is when the Bosnian Serb army attempted, as you said, to split Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, after that time, moving into the month of November, in the month of November, as you recall, were there convoys that went out of Sarajevo for purposes of delivering either people or aid?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were convoys going out of Sarajevo towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- there were many other convoys that UNHCR were delivering all around Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I do not recollect all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, right around that -- right around the 4th or 5th of November, do you recall there being negotiations between the Presidency, represented, I would take it by Izetbegovic; Pale represented, I would take it by Mr. Dr. Karadzic; and the Croatian represented by, I'm not sure, concerning convoys of buses of Serbs and Croats, Serbs leaving Sarajevo to Belgrade, Croats leaving Sarajevo to Split?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was there -- with regard to the representative for the Croatian side, which we've kind of touched upon lightly, but actually they were pretty much of an important consideration at that time, the representative for the Croatian side would that have been Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Bobetko was at that time in the Croatian Army General Staff, in other words, based out of Zagreb. The negotiations from the -- the first thing to say is the negotiations for that particular action were conducted between headquarter Sector Sarajevo or through the facilities of headquarter Sector Sarajevo rather than through my own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were dealing with -- they were dealing -- headquarter Sector Sarajevo had a Bosnian Serb liaison officer who was based at the Sarajevo PTT building which was the headquarter Sector Sarajevo who had communications through to Lukavica which was the military headquarters there. The Serb -- sorry, the Bosnian Croatian negotiator, I do not know who that was. My guess would be Colonel Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, after the negotiations in early November, I believe that there was another meeting that you had around the 14th of November, and that was a meeting that you had with General Galic, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't here today say, Yes, it was the 14th. But yes there was certainly a meeting with General -- there were a number of meetings that General Morillon had with General Galic around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me read you from the statement that I've read to you from before and see whether that refreshes your recollection with regard to that which you have said previously concerning the meeting with General Galic on the 14th. This would be page 10: "On 14 November we had a first meeting with General Stanislav Galic in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters at the Lukavica" -- my apologies, "... barracks outside Sarajevo close to the airport. Galic was not at the level of someone who Morillon would normally meet with." And I think there you are referring to once again the position rank matter that we've discussed previously which is people of -- I am sorry. Military men and women of equal rank in position meet with each not lower or higher?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "I believe Morillon was trying to get in touch with Mladic about agreement with the deployment of CanBat 2 to the Banja Luka area, but Morillon was having difficulty getting in touch with Mladic." Now, is this the same CanBat 2 discussion that had been going on probably since October?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And if you recall in March, I referred to a Canadian battalion stuck outside Zvornik; that was that same battalion five months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say there were a Canadian battalion stuck outside of Zvornik, was that close to the Zvornik bridge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as you went across the Zvornik bridge from the Bosnian side and entered the Serbian side, if you turned immediately left, there was a long road and parking area and the Canadian battalion which is lined up row upon row of vehicles with the soldiers just living on the vehicles and in little tents they pitched alongside their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have, I believe it's 1D00-2594, which is an aerial view of a bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, it's D22. My apologies. Defence 22. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I guess it is under seal that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies. I suppose we should -- I don't know why it is, but I suppose we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This bridge seems to have obtained an elusive quality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Chamber assume that as the picture stands north is north, south, east, west --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, Mladic, who Morillon was trying to get ahold of with regard to the CanBat deployment issue, was unavailable?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you learned that Mladic as a matter of fact was engaged in fighting, was he not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably in the aftermath of the last attempt to attack Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And is it your understanding that that's where Mladic was on the 14th? Because you say here: "I believe that Mladic was preoccupied dealing with his emergency down in south-east Bosnia where his forces were under sustained attack from the Croats."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a totally different matter. That was the attack in the, I can't remember the name of the place, I have it in my notes, I can point it out on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But with regard to the south-east portion of Bosnia where this attack was occurring, that was -- was that an attack involving only Croatian forces, or was that an attack that was involving a combination of Croatian forces and other forces, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no personnel in the area in order to verify one thing or the other. What Mladic told us was that it was a combination of Bosnian Croat forces reinforced by Republic of Croatia forces. In other words, forces commanded from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was there -- would that have been -- I'm mentioning an area to you to see if that refreshes your recollection. Would that have been Trevince?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And now, with regard to that particular battle, if I'm understanding correctly, Mladic was fighting two separate sets of forces at that time. One would have been Croatian forces, and the other would have been the army of the BiH, the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces; is that correct? He was fighting on two front?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, effectively it was three fronts because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Three fronts.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were the ABiH, in other words, the Muslim Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then from time to time he was also engaged in fighting with the HVO which was the Croatian -- sorry the Bosnian Croatian military, who at that time were, I believe, commanded by Brigadier General Petkovic. And then thirdly was with the HV who were the army of the Republic of Croatia, in other words, the army commanded and headquartered in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the information that you had, and I'm going back now to, for a minute, to the issue that he had raised in terms of being not on equal footing in terms of weaponry as opposed to infantry, did you have information with regard to the size of these various forces, and by that I mean the HVO, the Croatian Army, as you've articulated, and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similarly, we had intelligence assessments which had been prepared prior to our deployment and continued to be developed whilst we were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the ABiH had a very large number of people who by definition, because they were Yugoslav, had done national service and therefore knew how to use weapons. All of them, virtually any adult male in Bosnia and Yugoslavia knew how to use small arms. However, they didn't have that many small arms, and they had very very few heavy weapons. The HVO, which is the Croatian militia inside Bosnia, they were by comparison much better equipped, and they were equipped by the HV. And there was a clear communication line up from Split, up from the direction of Split, up into the centre of Bosnia through which the HVO had easy access to whatever equipment the Croatian authorities in Zagreb made available to them. The HV itself, the Republic of Croatia's military forces were even better equipped than the HVO, and were purchasing equipment on the international arms market and were having equipment made available to them from international arms sales.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the strength of those -- strength of those respective armies in terms of men or fighting soldiers, are you in a position to give us those numbers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a kind of meaningless question because literally any adult male could pick up a weapon and they all had items of military uniform. And it was often very difficult to identify what's a soldier as in a professional soldier who has been trained versus what is somebody who is actually a civilian, however, who has done military service and actually knows how to use a small arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Okay. So just in terms of a better understanding of that, with regard to those villages that were under pressure, as you've discussed, can you tell us in those villages how many of the villagers were either directly involved with the ABiH, under let's say for example the authority of Oric who was, I believe, the commander of that -- of the Srebrenica enclave, or who were fellow travellers, by that I mean were sympathetic to the Bosnia cause?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- and again I'm making estimates. This is not because I have specific information to say. The reality was that inside the Srebrenica enclave, the Muslims had very few small arms. Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm asking you about able-bodied fighting men, not about arms.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So can you then repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. The question as asked is precisely what Colonel Tucker was trying to answer. It's been reformulated now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's not. Can you tell us in those villages how many of the villagers were either directly involved with the ABiH, let's say, for example under the authority of Oric or who were fellow travellers? That has nothing to do with the issue of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is the distinct from the numerical strength of the HV, HVO, and ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, however when it's reformulated he's asking simply about the able bodied fighting men and trying to further limit. I believe that the witness should have the opportunity to answer the first question asked in regards to who was present in the village -- I'm sorry, inside of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you objecting because of the chronology of the questions, or are you objecting because the question itself is objectionable?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to the fact that the witness is not being able to answer the questions asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if he is not able to answer the questions asked, then he says, I'm not able to answer. Is that a ground of objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he wasn't -- he did not say that he could not answer the question. He began to answer the question, was cut off by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, and then was asked a separate question. And so we're asking for the witness to be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The prior question where he was cut off, okay, can you refer us to the transcript where that happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, it's at 76 starting at page 7 is the initial question -- I'm sorry. No, I'm sorry, that's a repeat. My apologies. The initial question is coming in at page 75 starting at line 15. He begins to answer at line 22, is cut off, and is asked a separate question starting on line 25. I would ask for the witness to be allowed to respond to the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the question that I asked, Colonel Tucker's answer was unresponsive. I'm happy to ask the same question again that I asked on page 75 in its verbatim form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Just ask it. Could you just ask the question instead of giving just the background information. If we ask short questions and we get short answers, we have our communication much more --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have testified that there were villages under pressure, and you have told us what you learned was the manner of attack by the Bosnian Serb forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to those villages that you've testified to being under pressure, can you tell us how many of the villagers were under the command of the ABiH Army in that area commanded by or Oric, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obviously do not have intelligence as to the numbers, as I was not at those villages. What I can say is that it is my understanding, which was also confirmed by Naser Oric when Morillon spoke with him, that the villages had in them the villagers plus on many occasions refugees who had fled to those villages. However, that there were no combatants in those villages. There was a second group of people who were combatants and who were, as you would describe it, in the chain of command as it were of Naser Oric, and the main determinant was the available of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But how many of those combatants were there, that were under Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would estimate it was probably several thousand around the perimeter of the Srebrenica enclave. But that's purely a personal estimate. It's not something we ever bothered to try and assess because it was to us meaningless information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in which villages specifically were these people located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people weren't located at villages. These people were located on the front line. And as the front line was moved as it was pressed back, obviously these people withdrew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I then understand you to be saying that your answer of several thousand combatants under Naser Oric is actually not answering Mr. Guy-Smith's question because now you are telling us of an estimate on the front line, not an estimate of the numbers in the villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The estimate of several thousand is for the entire Srebrenica pocket. I am not in a position to be able to say however many combatants there may or may not have been at any particular village at any particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I hope I haven't confused the issue further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think you have at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall the issue of convoys being sent to Srebrenica on the 17th of November between Morillon and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was when Mladic had told Morillon to provide a route, and he had or his staff had amended the route in order to try to ensure that it bypassed areas of difficulty. And there was a meeting around that time between General Morillon and General Mladic that I recall Mladic frequently getting up and going out of the meeting as he was getting updates from his own staff about the progress of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was a meeting in which you commented, and see whether or not this is accurate, once again referring to your statement, you say at page 11: "Lieutenant-General Mladic barely made any effort to conceal the the fact that nothing could or would happen in Bosnian Serb held BH without his specific approval. It was very apparent that he made all the practical military decisions that mattered."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the meeting that Mladic and Morillon had concerning convoys, something I think rather dramatic happened on the 17th of November, which is that the UNHCR suspended all deliveries of relief to Eastern Bosnia, both to Bosnian Serbs and other communities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, that happening. It was driven by a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to that, to put this into a context, what has occurred is prior to the UNHCR suspending the delivery of humanitarian aid, Mladic has imposed particular conditions upon the convoy being able to travel; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did lay a number of constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then independently in reaction to those constraints, the UNHCR made a determination that they would suspend the delivery of humanitarian aid because in their view it was necessary to have a global assessment of needs as well as a deeper statement of cooperation by authorities at a central and local level; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a loose description.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to what you said in your statement, and I've actually quoted what you said, which is: "The UNHCR suspend on 17th of November all deliveries of relief to Eastern Bosnia, both to Bosnian Serb and other communities pending a global assessment of needs as well as a deeper statement of cooperation by authorities at a central and local level."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more to it than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to deal with the issue here of the suspension. Because as I understand it what happened was that a letter was written by the UNHCR which indicated that a suspension would occur.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when the letter was written that indicated that a suspension would occur, at that point in time what was your reaction, by "your" I'm talking about Morillon and you obviously, to the independent action of the UNHCR to suspend understanding that they did that, of course, in light of what they understood to be Mladic's demands?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that Morillon was quite upset and quite angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there -- did there come as a result of this suspension a meeting between Morillon and the head of the UNHCR concerning the fact that humanitarian aid was being suspended by the very organisation that should be delivering it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morillon believed that it was his duty to keep trying to get aid going through regardless of whatever the obstacles or difficulties put in their place. UNHCR had the same belief but believed, and again I'm going by recollection from a long time ago, believed that they needed to take this stand temporarily in order to try and achieve the greater objective of getting freedom of movement, et cetera. And there's a disagreement between Morillon and UNHCR about the means to achieve the end, the end being that aid gets through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so what you have now is you have, as I understand it, three different views of how aid is to get through. You have the Mladic view of how aid is to get through, you have the Morillon view which is aid to get through at any cost, and I'm not -- excuse me, not at any cost, but aid -- get it through?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you have the UNHCR view that is that they are -- I'm making an assumption here, that they are an independent organisation and nobody is going to dictate in any fashion whatsoever how humanitarian aid is to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a fair summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. How long did UNHCR suspend the delivery of humanitarian aid as a result of their decision that they needed to take a stand with regard to this issue?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but what I do know is that before the end of November, humanitarian aid convoys were once again moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is as a matter of fact the convoy that leaves sometime around, I think, the 27th of November?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one particular convoy which went through to -- which eventually didn't succeed in getting through to Srebrenica. What I need to emphasise here is that we've been talking and focusing obviously on convoys to the enclaves, but there are dozens and dozens of other convoys going to other parts of Bosnia, and that we should not lose site of the fact that there are also many other UNHCR activities, not just these particular convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had earlier mentioned, and I just want to grab the point while it's fresh in the mind, you had earlier mentioned that your mandate was a mandate under, I believe, you said Chapter 6?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard you were not -- were not to engage in fighting, those are the words that you used, you said as a matter of fact on page 60: "Our mandate was not to engage in the fighting." I wanted to ask you about that, which is, when -- if you are aware of this, when the mandate changed from a Chapter 6 mandate to a Chapter 7 mandate, at that point didn't the mandate remain the same with regard to engaging in the fighting? Didn't the mandate remain as being a peacekeeping mandate as opposed to some other form of mandate which caused a whole series of other confusions ultimately, but from the outset the mandate was never for UNPROFOR to engage in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key difference is that under Chapter 6 in order to achieve whatever the mandate is in Chapter 6, you are not allowed to use force. Whereas under Chapter 7 the UN force is allowed to use force in order to achieve its mission. And that's the key difference between Chapter 6 and Chapter 7; it's the use of the permissibility of the UN to use force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So, it's your position that the UN can -- an UNPROFOR force can use some form of aggressive action in order to achieve the mandate of delivering of humanitarian aid, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under Chapter 7, however we were not operating under Chapter 7, we were operating under Chapter 6 which does not permit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you, Colonel Tucker, that that interpretation is a relatively novel one in terms of what we've seen in this trial and that we have heard a fair amount of testimony that the mandate under Chapter 7 was peacekeeping and the only time that aggressive force could be used was in self-Defence, would that -- would you disagree with that interpretation of the mandate under Chapter 7?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under Chapter 6, self-Defence was, of course, also permitted; but under Chapter 6 we were not allowed to take any actions on one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think you've answered my question, sir, my question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that asking the witness to explain in expertise on Chapter 7 of the UN mandate is inappropriate. He has described what his personal experiences were under Chapter 6, to go forward and ask him to render opinions on Chapter 7 would go outside the province of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I believe that he has made a very clear distinction with regard to what his mandate was under Chapter 6, and he recognizes that he would have had a different ability and a different position under Chapter 7. And it's for that reason that I'm asking that question. Because when he initially answered the question, he mentioned that he did not have the mandate to engage in fighting, which I found to be curious strange since the articulated mandate under Chapter 7 didn't allow for UNPROFOR forces to be allowed in fighting either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess, Mr. Guy-Smith, the point here is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess the point here is that obviously Mr. -- beg your pardon Colonel Tucker is not testifying as an expert on the mandate of the UNPROFOR. That's his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's all I can do is ask him for his understanding. I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think he has given it to you, he says under Chapter 7 they can bull-doze to deliver aid. Under Chapter 6 they cannot; they can only defend themselves. So his understanding is that Chapter 7, you can defend yourself, you can bull-doze to open your way for humanitarian aid. Under Chapter 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I guess you can shoot too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bull-doze meaning aggression. Under Chapter 6 it's only self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If that's his understanding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you returned to the crisis headquarters, were you made aware of any of the rules of engagement that had been imposed on the UNPROFOR forces during the time in Sarajevo and the region?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at the crisis management headquarters, that was 1996. That was after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the NATO deployment, which was under totally different rules of engagement. The -- when I was in Bosnia in 1992/1993 we were under Chapter 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, my question is very simply. When you were at the crisis headquarters, were you made aware of the rules of engagement that existed in Sarajevo for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not part of the -- we were interested in the rules of engagement under which the NATO force, which was deployed to Bosnia, had to operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, it will be helpful if you just answer the question and stop there. Don't volunteer information about NATO because that's not the question. The question is about UNPROFOR. You were not given those -- you were not made aware of the rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was a meeting, now I'm back in a meeting with Mladic, Karadzic, and General Morillon, that would have been the 27th of November, 1992, in which again the issue of CanBat, the deployment of CanBat came up. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that meeting, Karadzic affirmed the position that Mladic had taken the day before that the question of the deployment of CanBat 2 to Banja Luka was to be discussed at an assembly session; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that once he had gotten an answer from his assembly, he would get back to you with regard to that issue?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in that meeting there was a discussion in which Dr. Karadzic and Morillon agreed on the route for the convoy to Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as a result of that agreement between Morillon and Karadzic, I take it that Morillon then went back to the UNHCR and said, Listen, we have a way of getting humanitarian aid through that area; could you please reconsider your suspension and fire up the trucks? I'm being somewhat colloquial, but I think you get the intent of my question.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm when UNHCR lifted -- I can't confirm specifically when UNHCR lifted their suspension that you referred to a number of minutes ago. What I can confirm is that a convoy left -- it was a UNHCR convoy and that it eventually got through to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ultimately Karadzic did get back to you with regard to the issue of deployment of CanBat 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what occurred was that the assembly did not, as I understand it, approve the deployment of CanBat 2 along the lines that had been discussed and once again placed some other conditions with regard to what government or governments would engage in the transportation of CanBat 2?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember here sat now of what the reasons for the -- but I do know that -- I can confirm that the answer was no and some other conditions were laid down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And is the statement that you -- is the statement that you previously made that, once again referring to the statement that we have been talking about on 28th November, the first UN convoy to reach Srebrenica since the beginning of the war arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "The overall impression that we had at this point as a regards the Bosnian Serbs' objective was that they now wanted peace. They thought the war was over and were primarily interested in consolidation and recognition of what they had." Right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would -- that would fall into line with the discussion that we were having earlier with regard to the issue of cessation of hostilities agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that also falls into line with the discussion that we've had concerning how the differing parties, and by that I mean the Bosnian Serbs and the Presidency viewed the issue of cease-fire and peace?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I think it would be fair to say obviously that as a result of what happens in the ensuing days, by that I mean within a very short period of time, the Presidency is not of the same mind with regard to the issue of peace because as a matter of fact they once again begin an aggressive action with regard to breaking out of Sarajevo in the early part of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I keep on having this voice behind me saying 1992, which I think is a good thing. Okay. Now, in terms of what we have now is some humanitarian aid coming through. We've had some success in that regard, which I take it you are pleased with, I mean not totally satisfied, but at least this is a move in the right direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have a clear impression based upon the meetings that you've had with Mladic and Karadzic that they are interested at that time in reaching a peaceful solution; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you have the exact opposite view from the Presidency, which is they are not quite ready for peace because -- go ahead, sorry.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not ready for peace, because the peace that the Bosnian Serbs were trying to impose was seized through force of arms and they did not accept or agree what had been seized through force of arms and were therefore trying to continue and redress the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what's happening with the Croatian contingent now?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian contingent are sitting fairly quiet at the moment watching what's going on. There had been some nasty fighting between the Croatian -- sorry, the Bosnian Croats and the Muslim Croats in September and October down in the -- down south of Vitez, but that had stopped by the time of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the state of affairs in Sarajevo, which I think you have discussed with us. You've indicated that it was bitterly cold, I believe?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that there was difficulty with the delivery in situ of gas and electricity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that issue, in the same manner that Bosnian forces -- or I should put it in other terms, let me start over again. In the same manner that there had been aggressive acts by trucks with mortars near Kosevo Hospital, there also was a local decision by Bosniaks in Sarajevo to limit the delivery of electricity and fuel, something which you discussed with Judge Orie as being a predicate to the exploitation of misery. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to this specific issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just clear this -- okay. Before we clear it, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would just like that page citation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are looking for the page citation, did the witness discuss with Judge Orie somewhere in the corridors, or is this a Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh it's -- no, I don't think he had a discussion with Judge Orie in the corridors that I would know about. This is something that is discussed in trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think. Let's place it on the record that it was a discussion with Judge Orie in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to IT-98-29-T, and I'll be dealing with a couple of different pages. But with regard to the particular issue that we are discussing right now, that would be page 10.030 where you were asked the following questions by Judge Orie, and the following responses ensued: Judge Orie, starting at line 9: "I'm trying to understand this. The supplies of water, electricity, and gas also served their own population, referring to the Presidency authorities. What was the specific reason why they would play tricks which would result in not restoring the supplies when their own population would suffer from it? Do you have any explanation about that?" And your response, Colonel Tucker: "I do have an explanation and it is as follows: There were elements within the Bosnian leadership who believed that the only way to take back that which had been taken from them by the Bosnian Serbs, that could only happen by either international intervention in Bosnia or by the provision of arms and ammunition to Bosnia, which was not possible at that time because of the arms embargo. Those people believed that the only way to secure such international assistance was to depict the situation in Sarajevo to be so severe that the international community would be willing to intervene. Therefore, it was not in their interest to see any improvement in the situation in Sarajevo. It was not in their interest to see any -- to see the lot of the civilian population improve. To put it bluntly, the more suffering, the better because that played to the television cameras and would ultimately lead to the pressure that they wanted in order to achieve international intervention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Would that be, in three words, exploitation of misery?" Your answer, Colonel Tucker: "Could you say that again, sir?"

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Judge Orie: "Would that be, in three words, exploitation of misery?" Answer: "Absolutely, sir." I take it you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The only thing I would say is that that was some elements, not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. As 1992 went to rest, that's 1992, and 1993 came into the fore, you began to receive some relatively strong complaints from the Bosnian Serbs with regard to attacks on them and attacks on Serbian villagers in the area such as the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And those attacks were attacks that were emanating from Naser Oric's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were originating from Naser Oric's command, I cannot confirm. What I can confirm is that the Bosnian Serbs claimed that these attacks were originating out of the enclaves, and that Naser Oric was in command in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, one of the things that they were -- was being brought to your attention was a massacre of some Serb civilians, I believe in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, shortly thereafter you began to receive information from the Presidency -- before I go there, I take it that with regard to that information did you or Morillon make arrangements in January when you received this information to go to the region to determine the accuracy or the validity of those complaints at that time in January?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in January, because what happened in January is that central Bosnia blew up between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It did indeed. In February you received some information, I believe from, among others, President Izetbegovic and Ganic with regard to the massacre at Cerska, and that massacre included relatively strong allegations with regards to people being put in houses and burned, the entire village was burned to the ground, that some 700 wounded or more, and I'm not sure about the figure --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- were in that particular village and this needed your attention?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's essentially correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And President Izetbegovic and Ganic made arrangements with the -- and I'm asking here, the war committee in Srebrenica to facilitate, at least from their standpoint, your entry into Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm whether they made arrangements, with whom they made arrangements. They simply told General Morillon that they would inform the people inside the enclave that General Morillon was going to try and come into the enclave in order to see for himself what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, by that point in time, by that I mean in February of 1993, had you seen the radio communication centre at the PTT building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you mean the radio communication centre in the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To which the answer is yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
