utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that particular communication centre was, I think is, as you've perhaps put it previously, well equipped, strong, it may not have been the most up-to-date system, but it was a system that certainly could handle sophisticated communications?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Presidency building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you, and I'm jumping ahead now for a moment, when you got to Srebrenica, there ultimately came a time when you were shown the same kind of radio communication centre that I believe was in -- was it the PTT building of the Srebrenica which was the headquarters of the war committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't the same as the setup in Sarajevo, but it was still a pretty comprehensive setup. It wasn't as large as the one in the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, what occurred with regard to you becoming aware of that radio communication centre was that when the decision was made for Morillon to make the speech which you alluded to earlier speaking to Ms. Carter, some journalists had indicated to you or told you that this particular radio communication centre existed, something that you did not know beforehand, not information that had been shared with you by either the war committee or Naser Oric; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If I remember correctly, the journalists were actually permitted by the war committee to use the radio equipment in order to communicate their dispatches back to Sarajevo for ultimate publication to their newspapers, radios, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you decided to go into the Srebrenica area, you made arrangements to get there by way of a helicopter; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where did that helicopter leave from and where did it land in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a French national helicopter which was assigned to United Nations which took off from Kiseljak and then flew to Tuzla and landed in Tuzla and we got off the helicopter in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the - and I'm not sure what you call them, I guess it would be the coordinates or the route - was there at that time a recognised, I don't know what you call it, air route or air bridge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Air corridor, thank you so much. Was there a recognised air corridor into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was only an air corridor to Tuzla. Which is why -- that's where we were dropped off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And was that an air corridor that you frequented? That UNPROFOR frequently used?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the first time it was used was when we flew from Kiseljak to Tuzla in order to go into Konjevic Polje. The second time that that air corridor was used was when we went from Kiseljak to Tuzla in order to go into Srebrenica itself. Those were the first and second times that that corridor was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue, because there two issues we have -- well, there are many issues we have on this trip, but there are two, I think, major issues that have been brought to your attention by the various sides. One is the massacre at Kravica and the other is the massacre at Cerska. Right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two massacres at Cerska that I mentioned. The first is the allegation by the -- by Izetbegovic and Ganic that people have been locked in houses and the houses burnt down and killed in the houses. The second was an allegation by the Bosnian Serbs that Serbs had been massacred by the Muslims in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to -- and I'm now going to jump ahead for a moment. I believe it was on the 22nd of March you attended a funeral, but sometime around the 22nd of March you were shown a series of bodies that were decomposed bodies that the Bosnian Serbs indicated to you were the people who had been massacred; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were shown firstly to the site where the excavations were going on and there were forensic investigations going on and we saw these investigations going on, saw a number of decomposing bodies, and we were shown the building in which one of the survivors of the massacre claimed he had seen Bosnian Muslims killing these Bosnian Serb villagers. We were then after that taken to the funeral which was actually in, in fact, it was on the outskirts of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that particular incident, and by that I mean your viewing of the bodies and your going to the particular crime scenes, you did not make any specific reports with regard to that visit that you made to the crime scene in Kravica because that wasn't your mission or your task; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did report what had happened, what we had seen, and it was again part of the radio communications that I've described previously. And we indeed reported this to the headquarters, BH command back in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, so I understand, with regard to the crime scene that you went to, you made no specific report about that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I reported that we had been to this scene at Kravica, that the Serbs had made these allegations to us about what had happened, and I repeated those allegations, and they were reported to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you can be of some help to me in that regard. Apart from the first statement that we've been discussing, you also made a statement on the 20th and 21st of September, 2002, and the 1st and 2nd of November, 2002, in which you said on page 16 of that statement: "I did not make any specific report with regard to the visit that we made to this crime scene in Kravica. The reason for this was that our mission and task in Bosnia was not to gather evidence, but to ensure humanitarian aid reached those in need and to support all efforts to reduce the bloodshed and prove the safety of the civilian population in the region." You go on to say more, and I want to be fair to you because I can tell you exactly what you said. "Furthermore, in my view there was little substance to record. In general, I sent reports to Kiseljak at least daily and on occasion every two hours. Other than the report, we had visited Kravica, I do not believe I gave any specific details in those reports." So as I understand it, with regard to the issue of there being a specific report concerning the -- what had been characterised as a massacre of Serbian villagers, you did not memorialise that in any fashion at the time of the event other than the oral reporting that you made?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did was, if I remember correctly, was provide a report of what had happened that day. On that day, this visit had taken place and I reported that we had conducted this visit. And that we had been to this -- the scene of this alleged massacre. And that we had seen bodies. What I did not do was try and collect legal evidence as to what had or had not happened because that -- the collection of legal evidence in order to support subsequent prosecution, that's what I meant was not part of my task and objective at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I was trying to understand what you meant when you said you did not make a specific report, you clarified that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make a legally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A legal inspection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A legal inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the other area that -- the Cerska area, you didn't go to Cerska, did you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the outskirts of Cerska, it was Morillon himself who physically went into the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And before he went into the village, you had, apart from meeting with Izetbegovic and Ganic who had told you about the horrors that had occurred, you also spoke, I believe, with Naser Oric about that when you were in Srebrenica and Oric - would it be fair to say? - echoed the same, which is that people were burned in houses and that there were hundreds, 700 or more, who had been wounded; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your mixing up two separate events. The issue of being burnt in houses, Naser Oric echoed. The issue of the claim that there were 700 or so wounded in Konjevic Polje, that was a claim which was made by Izetbegovic and Ganic, which was one of the reasons leading to General Morillon's decision to go there to investigate the actual situation on the grounds himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Above and beyond Izetbegovic Ganic and Oric, you also had occasion to speak with a Bosniak commander in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who also gave you that same information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was also very specific about the accusation of people being burned in houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from those individuals who you mentioned, did anybody else on the Bosniak side, which I will call for, as you have, the Presidency side, give you further information concerning the burning of people in houses, or are we left with Izetbegovic, Ganic --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Izetbegovic, Ganic, the Bosniak commander in Tuzla, and Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Morillon went to Cerska, he examined the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He made a number of determinations about what occurred, one, there had been heavy fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Two, the number of wounded was not in the neighbourhood of 700 but rather much less?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the number of wounded which we found in Konjevic Polje. It wasn't actually General Morillon who determined that. It was somebody from Medicins Sans Frontieres who went around all the houses in Konjevic Polje in order to triage the injured for evacuation, and it was he who came back and said there are not 700 here, there are about 70 here. 700 is a specific number, the 70 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was 73 give or take a couple.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of people being burned, Morillon said --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I refer the Court and counsel to IT-03-68 page 5831, starting at line 15 of your examination by Mr. Di Fazio of the Office of the Prosecutor: "Q. Did he report any bodies in houses that had been burned? "A. General Morillon said that he had unfortunately -- that he was unfortunately familiar with the smell of burnt human flesh and that he had walked around the village and that he had not smelled that smell and that he had not seen anything which indicated that anyone had been burnt or there had been people burnt inside houses." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time. And before we move, let me just indicate that ID00-8093 was not tendered. Was that your intension?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, we obviously haven't finished today. It looks like we had been scheduled to finish today with this witness. We may have difficulties tomorrow with interpreters. We may not be able to sit a full session. How much longer are you likely to be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe based upon what I see here that I have any -- that I have -- I don't believe I have much more than a session. I believe I can get it done in a session, I think with a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With a bit of thought over the evening. I will do what I can to make sure that my hopes become a reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we impress on you to do those thoughts tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will then adjourn to tomorrow, but before we do so, Colonel Tucker, I must again warn you, it's my duty unfortunately, but I do know you know it you are not supposed to talk to anybody about the case, not even your counsel, until you are excused from the witness-stand. Court stands adjourned to tomorrow 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
